blog.title: The denominator decides: why an 80 % reliable witness gets you to 41 %
blog.dek: Kahneman’s cab problem, counted on one picture of 1,000 cabs instead of solved with a formula.

sections.heading: The question
sections.caption: Before anything is counted: the witness says Blue. What is the chance it was?
sections.text:
A cab hit someone at night and drove off. A witness says the cab was Blue. The court, being careful, tested her under the same night conditions: shown cabs one at a time, she named the colour right 80 times in 100, and she was just as good with Blue cabs as with Green ones. In this city, 150 of the 1,000 cabs are Blue and the other 850 are Green.

What is the chance the cab was Blue?

Before you read on, write down a number. The point of the exercise is not to be right on the first try. It is to notice where your first answer came from, because the same reflex is at work every time someone hands you an accuracy figure and asks you to act on it.

sections.heading: The obvious answer, fairly put
sections.caption: Run that model and it says 80 %, with confidence.
sections.text:
The most common answer is 80 % (Kahneman, *Thinking, Fast and Slow*, chapter 16). It has a real argument behind it, and it deserves to be stated fairly: she is right 80 % of the time, so when she says Blue she is probably right, about 80 % of the time.

That model is not foolish. It gives exactly the right answer in one kind of city: a city where Blue and Green cabs are equally common. It is the answer your intuition reaches for because the witness is vivid and specific, and the city is a dull statistic in the background. Kahneman’s point is that we let the vivid, causal story crowd out the statistical one.

The trouble is that this model never looked at this city.

sections.heading: What it ignored
sections.caption: But it never looked at the city: 850 of the 1,000 cabs are Green.
sections.text:
Eight hundred and fifty of the 1,000 cabs are Green. The witness is the same witness, with the same eyes and the same 80 %; what changes is the set of cabs she could be describing.

A “Blue” can come from two places: a Blue cab seen right, or a Green cab seen wrong. With so many Green cabs on the road, the second source is not small. Her error rate is low, but it is applied to a large group, and a small fraction of a large group can outnumber a large fraction of a small one. That is the whole trick, and it is easier to see than to say.

sections.heading: Count it
sections.caption: Count the Blue ones among them: 120 of 290. About 41 %, not 80 %.
sections.text:
Instead of a formula, test her on every cab in the city, one dot per cab.

- Of the 150 Blue cabs, she calls 150 × 0.8 = **120** Blue.
- Of the 850 Green cabs, she calls 850 × 0.2 = **170** Blue.

So 290 cabs would be called Blue, and only those 290 are still in question: the rest stay in the city, faint, but they are no longer part of the answer. The Blue ones are 120 of them: **120 ÷ 290 = 41 %**.

Most of us land near 80; the count says 41, a gap of 39 points. This is Bayes’ rule, done by counting natural frequencies instead of multiplying conditional probabilities. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage showed in 1995 that when the same problem is posed as counts of people (or cabs) rather than percentages, far more people get it right. The film never shows the formula; it shows the denominator forming.

sections.heading: One difference
sections.caption: What differs: only the base rate. 41 % in one city, 80 % in the other.
sections.text:
To see which part of the problem does the work, split the city in two and change exactly one thing. City A is the textbook’s: 15 % Blue. City B is hypothetical: half its cabs are Blue. Same witness, same 80 %, same way of counting, same seed for the dots.

In City A the count is 120 of 290, 41 %. In City B it is 400 of 500, 80 %. Nothing about the witness changed between the two halves; only the base rate did. So the common answer is the right answer only in a city that is half Blue. Answering 80 % in City A means answering as if the city were half Blue. That is base-rate neglect: not a lack of arithmetic, but a silent swap of the city you are in for a simpler one.

sections.heading: Where this stops
sections.text:
The film is honest about its own edges, and so is this post:

- It is a classroom problem: the dots draw the stated proportions, not data.
- It assumes the witness’s errors are independent of everything else: the light, the street, which cabs drive at night.
- The 80 % reliability is the textbook’s, measured under night conditions.
- City B is hypothetical; the textbook’s city is 15 % Blue.

None of these change the lesson; they change how far you can carry the exact numbers. In a real case you would want the actual base rate for the time and place, and a reliability measured under the conditions that matter.

sections.heading: One question for you
sections.caption: Count it: 40 Blue cabs called Blue, 190 Green cabs called Blue. 40 of 230.
sections.text:
Same witness, but now only 5 % of the cabs are Blue. Is the chance that a “Blue” call is right above or below 41 %? Answer before you scroll.

<details><summary>The count</summary>

In a city of 1,000 with 50 Blue cabs: 50 × 0.8 = 40 Blue cabs get called Blue, and 950 × 0.2 = 190 Green cabs do too. That is 40 of 230, about 17 %. The rarer the Blue cabs, the less a “Blue” means.

</details>

sections.heading: Back to the case
sections.text:
A witness says the cab was Blue. The chance it was Blue is 41 %, not 80 %. The witness doesn’t decide; the city does.

The same structure sits under every accuracy figure you are handed: a highly accurate test for a rare condition, an alert that is usually right about a rare fault, a model with a high score on a rare class, a reference check on a rare kind of fraud. In each case the question to ask first is the one the cab problem teaches: how many of each are out there? Before you trust the signal, count the base rate. **The denominator decides.**
